title: Numbers that tell a story
goal: Report figures the way Indonesian reports do — *meningkat sebesar*, *menurun menjadi*, *tercatat*, *dibandingkan dengan* — write numbers with the Indonesian comma and point, and talk a board through a chart without either hiding the bad news or drowning in it.
bekal: describe a trend precisely: *meningkat sebesar 35 persen*, *turun dari 80 menjadi 68*, *tercatat 4,6*
write numbers, decimals and money correctly: *4,6*, *1.250*, *Rp4,2 miliar*
present a chart and answer questions about it: *Grafik ini menunjukkan…*, *Seperti terlihat pada…*

notes: **Sebesar vs menjadi.** *Meningkat sebesar 35 persen* is “rose **by** 35 per cent”; *meningkat menjadi 324* is “rose **to** 324”. Mixing them up changes the figure, so reports often give both, exactly as Sarah does. *Sebanyak* does the same job as *sebesar* for things you count: *bertambah sebanyak 84 orang*.

**Dibanding and dibandingkan dengan.** Yoga's *dibanding triwulan pertama* is fine in speech; the report wants the full *dibandingkan dengan triwulan sebelumnya*. ⚠️ Don't write *dibandingkan daripada* — *daripada* belongs with *lebih* (*lebih tinggi daripada*), not with *dibandingkan*.

**Signifikan** is borrowed from English and fully naturalised (note the Indonesian spelling, *-kan* not *-cant*). In reports it usually just means “sizeable”; in a research paper it means statistically significant, so Dr. Lestari would raise an eyebrow at Sarah's loose use.

💬 **Doang** is Jakarta for *saja* or *hanya* (“just, only”) and always comes after the thing it limits: *dua belas orang doang*. Never in writing. Its sister *aja* is milder and acceptable in informal messages; *doang* has a slightly dismissive ring.

**Tercatat** — “is recorded as” — is how reports present a figure without claiming credit or blame for it. *Tercatat 4,6* sounds neutral and factual; *kami berhasil mencapai 4,6* sounds like marketing. Boards and journalists both prefer the former.

**Realisasi anggaran** is the share of a budget actually spent. Indonesian organisations report it religiously, and a figure much below 90 per cent invites the question *Kenapa anggarannya tidak terserap?* (“Why wasn't the budget absorbed?”) — underspending is treated as a planning failure, not thrift.

grammars.title: Up, down and flat: the trend verbs
body: Everyday Indonesian says *naik* and *turun*; reports prefer the *me-* verbs and, even more, their nouns. Learn them in pairs, because a good report sentence usually contains one of each.
after: The noun lets you pack the figure into the subject: *Peningkatan jumlah peserta disebabkan oleh kelas daring* (“The increase in participants was due to the online classes”). That is Unit 2's nominalisation at work.
*Anjlok* is vivid and slightly journalistic — fine in a headline, too dramatic for a board report. *Merosot* sits between the two.

grammars.title: Writing numbers the Indonesian way
body: Indonesia uses the European system: the comma is the decimal separator and the point groups thousands. Getting this wrong in a report is not a style slip; it changes the value by a factor of a thousand.
after: ⚠️ *Miliar* is the English billion (a thousand million); *triliun* is the English trillion. *Rp* is written straight before the figure with no space.

EYD rules: numbers that take one or two words are spelled out in running text (*lima belas persen*, *dua sekolah*), but in tables, data and a series of figures you use digits. And never begin a sentence with digits: write *Dua ratus empat puluh peserta…* or rephrase.

notes: **Grafik berikut menunjukkan…** and **Seperti terlihat (pada grafik)…** are the two standard ways to open a chart. *Berikut* (“the following”) points forward; *tersebut* (“the said”) points back to something already mentioned: *grafik tersebut*.

**Tajam** is literally “sharp” (a knife), and describes a steep rise or fall: *kenaikan tajam*, *penurunan tajam*. The gentle opposite is *landai* (a gentle slope) or *perlahan*. *Stagnan* means stuck, and is never good news.

**Terdampak** — “affected, hit by” — is a newer word that has almost pushed out *terkena dampak* in the news: *warga terdampak banjir*, *sekolah terdampak gempa*. It belongs to the same *ter-* family you met in B1, the one that happens to you.

**Diperkirakan and diproyeksikan.** Both mean “is expected”. *Diperkirakan* is the general word (also for weather); *diproyeksikan* sounds more technical, as if someone ran a model. Sarah uses *kami perkirakan* — the object-first passive — to own the estimate without sounding boastful.

**Per 30 Juni** means “as of 30 June”. *Per* also gives rates: *per orang*, *per semester*, *Rp50.000 per jam*. In finance you will see *kuartal* (quarter) alongside its more Indonesian twin *triwulan*; government documents prefer *triwulan*.

**Siap, Pak.** Literally “ready, sir”, it is how Indonesian offices say “will do”. It started in the military and police and is now everywhere, from ministries to start-ups. From a subordinate it is perfectly respectful; from a director like Sarah to her chairman it is also a small show of deference.

grammars.title: Talking a room through a chart
body: A chart presentation in Indonesian follows a predictable path: say what the chart shows, point to the peak and the low, give the cause, give the outlook. These phrases carry you through.

head: Phrase
English
rows: As you can see on the chart…

after: ⚠️ *Sebagian besar* is the natural “most of”; *kebanyakan* is fine in speech. Avoid *mayoritas dari peserta* — the *dari* is an English calque; just say *mayoritas peserta*.

blocks.text: Reports mix exact figures with fractions and hedges. The fractions use *per-* between the two numbers, and the approximations are the ones you met in A2 in a more formal suit.

*Lipat* is a fold: *dua kali lipat* is twofold, *tiga kali lipat* threefold. *Naik dua kali lipat* (doubled) is one of the most useful phrases in any report — and one of the most exaggerated in the news.

sections.title: The verbs of a report, from dull to dramatic

blocks.text: Choose the verb to fit the size of the change and the seriousness of the document. The words on the right belong in headlines, not in the minutes of a board meeting.

blocks.title: Three habits of a good Indonesian report
items: Give the base and the result, not just the percentage: *dari 80 menjadi 68 (turun 15%)*.
Name the period you compare with: *dibandingkan dengan periode yang sama tahun lalu*.
State the source and the cut-off date: *Sumber: basis data internal, per 30 Juni*.
